missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that weight can be treated as acting at a single point, the centre of mass. The phrase 'centre of mass' appears only in keyPoints[1].content ('Field lines point towards the centre of the mass'), with a different meaning.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
missing_spec_content.why: W = mg is given, but the lesson never states that weight is directly proportional to mass.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should recognise and be able to use the symbol for proportionality, ∝
missing_spec_content.why: The proportionality symbol ∝ (for example W ∝ m) is not introduced anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say how weight is measured. There is no mention of a calibrated spring-balance or newtonmeter.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe the similarities and distinctions between the planets, their moons, and artificial satellites.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not compare planets, moons and artificial satellites. 'Satellites' and 'moons' are mentioned only in passing, for example intro: 'moons in orbit around planets'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never explains that in a circular orbit the speed stays constant while the velocity changes because the direction changes. keyPoints[2].content mentions 'tangential velocity' and the centripetal force but does not make this point.

above_gcse.text: Near Earth's surface, the field is roughly uniform (the same strength and direction everywhere near the surface). ... The gravitational field is shown by field lines pointing towards the centre of the mass. They show the direction of the force on a small test mass.
above_gcse.why: Gravitational field lines, uniform versus radial fields and 'test mass' are not in the specification sections. This is A-level-style field treatment and could confuse a GCSE student.

above_gcse.text: Higher orbits: the gravitational field is weaker, so gravity provides less centripetal force. So a lower speed is needed to stay in orbit. A higher orbit also has a longer circumference. So the orbital period (the time for one orbit) is longer.
above_gcse.why: The specification only requires that 'for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes'. The direction of the speed–radius relationship and the idea of orbital period go beyond the specification text.

above_gcse.text: Orbital period: The time taken for one complete orbit — longer for higher orbits
above_gcse.why: Orbital period is not part of the specification sections given.

above_gcse.text: Don't just say 'gravity keeps it going round'. Say 'gravity provides the centripetal force needed for circular motion'.
above_gcse.why: The term 'centripetal force' does not appear in the specification sections. The specification wording is 'Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites ... to maintain their circular orbits'. Telling students they must use 'centripetal' adds a requirement the specification does not make.

wrong_terms.text: Weight is a force (N), and changes depending on gravity.
wrong_terms.spec_term: The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.

wrong_terms.text: Weight is in N and depends on gravity.
